content: 1. The documentation for BLE G.075 includes the design, construction, technical system architecture, and testing documentation. This is intended to support future configurations and adaptations of the solution for other health intervention initiatives. 2. The Digital Adaptation Kit for child health in emergencies provides a structured framework for implementing digital health interventions in emergency settings. 3. The Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG) offers guidance on integrating digital interventions into health programs. It is available at the WHO repository. 4. The Global Strategy on Digital Health 2020–2025 outlines a roadmap for leveraging digital technologies to strengthen health systems globally. 5. The Roadmap for Health Measurement and Accountability (MA4Health) by the World Bank Group, USAID, and WHO provides a unified agenda for health data and accountability in the post-2015 era. 6. The USAID Digital Strategy 2020–2024 outlines approaches to harness digital tools for health system strengthening and service delivery. 7. The Global Fund's Strategic Framework for Data Use for Action and Improvement at Country Level (2017–2022) emphasizes the importance of data-driven decision-making in health systems. 8. WHO's recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening provide evidence-based guidance for implementing digital health solutions. 9. The Shared Language for Digital Health document standardizes terminology for describing the use of digital technologies in health. 10. Barton et al. demonstrated the collect once, use many principle by integrating public health secondary data use requirements into an existing domain analysis model. 11. The WHO SMART guidelines aim to optimize the use of guideline recommendations at the country level in the digital age, as detailed in The Lancet Digital Health. 12. Boxwala et al. proposed a multi-layered framework for disseminating knowledge for computer-based decision support in health informatics. 13. The UHC Compendium serves as a repository of interventions for achieving universal health coverage, categorized by program area. 14. The National eHealth Strategy Toolkit provides a comprehensive guide for developing national eHealth strategies. 15. WHO's Optimize MNH recommendations focus on task-shifting to improve access to maternal and newborn health interventions. 16. The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) chart booklet provides guidance on managing childhood illnesses, including care for sick young infants up to 2 months of age. 17. The Management of the Sick Young Infant Aged Up to 2 Months participant manual offers detailed instructions for healthcare providers. 18. The IMCI distance learning course supports healthcare workers in managing childhood illnesses through remote education. 19. The Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) guidelines provide protocols for triaging and managing pediatric emergencies. 20. The guideline on the prevention and management of wasting and nutritional edema addresses acute malnutrition in children. 21. The Pocket Book of Hospital Care for Children offers clinical guidelines for managing common childhood illnesses in hospital settings. 22. The Caring for Newborns and Children in the Community guide supports community-level management of childhood illnesses. 23. WHO's classification of health workers maps occupations to the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO). 24. The International Labour Organization's ISCO provides a standardized framework for classifying occupations globally. 25. HL7 FHIR Release 5 outlines data types and standards for health information interoperability. 26. The Object Management Group's Decision Model and Notation (DMN) provides a framework for decision-making processes in health informatics. 27. The guide on developing health management information systems offers practical advice for low-resource settings. 28. The Public Health Informatics Institute's Collaborative Requirements Development Methodology (CRDM) supports the design of health information systems. 29. When adapting a data dictionary, modifications or additions to data elements may be necessary due to the structure of existing paper registers or local reporting requirements. 30. Data elements should have unique identification codes across the project, and their labels should be clear and understandable for end users. 31. The digital system should streamline processes and link duplicated data elements, ensuring consistency and efficiency. 32. Data types should align with HL7 FHIR standards, and multiple-choice fields should be clearly labeled and classified. 33. Validation requirements, editability, and the necessity of data fields should be clearly defined to optimize data flows and ensure accountability. 34. Conditional fields should include skip logic based on preset thresholds, and aggregate indicators should be specified where applicable. 35. Notes on inconsistencies or issues in data field definitions should be documented for resolution through team discussions. 36. The digital system should not merely replace paper registers but enhance processes and improve data management. 37. References include WHO guidelines, IMCI resources, and international standards for health data and workforce classification.
